title: Thermal vs. Bond Paper: Which Receipt Paper Should You Use?
description: Thermal rolls print fast and clean; bond paper resists heat and light. Here's how to choose the right receipt paper for each printer.
body:
Every receipt printer runs on one of two types of paper — thermal or bond — and using the wrong one turns a reliable machine into a source of jams, faded tickets, and angry customers. The good news: choosing correctly is simple once you know which printer you have and where the receipt lives. Here's how to match the paper to the job.

How Each Paper Works

Thermal paper is chemically coated. The printhead applies heat directly to the paper, which turns the coating dark to form text and barcodes — no ribbon, no ink, no toner. That's why thermal printers are fast, quiet, and cheap to run: the only consumable is the roll itself.

Bond paper is plain, uncoated paper. A bond (or impact) printer strikes the paper through an ink ribbon to leave marks, similar to an old typewriter. Because it physically presses ink into the paper, the image is more durable — but the printer has moving parts and needs ribbon replacements.

Key Differences That Matter for Hospitality

  • Print quality: Thermal output is crisp and dark immediately; bond output is lighter and relies on ribbon condition.
  • Durability: Bond ink resists heat and light, so it holds up on a sunny counter or near a heat lamp. Thermal can fade when exposed to direct heat, sunlight, or certain chemicals over time.
  • Cost and upkeep: Thermal has a higher per-roll price but no ribbon to buy or replace. Bond rolls are cheaper up front, but you'll also buy ribbons and manage wear on the printhead.
  • Speed and noise: Thermal prints fast and quietly; impact printers are slower and noticeably louder.

When to Choose Thermal

Thermal is the default for most modern hospitality setups — customer receipts, bar tabs, takeout tickets, and card terminals all print on thermal. It's the right call when you value speed and low maintenance, and when the receipt isn't sitting in direct heat or sunlight for long stretches.

When Bond Still Makes Sense

Bond paper earns its place in specific, high-durability situations. Kitchen tickets near grills and heat lamps, or receipts customers carry in a wallet or glove box for weeks, hold up better on bond because the ink won't fade under heat or light. If your operation prints documents that need to last — or that must survive a hot, bright environment — bond is worth the extra upkeep.

How to Confirm What Your Printer Needs

Check the label or manual on your printer for the paper spec. Most receipt printers list the exact roll width and whether they're thermal or impact. A quick test also works: run your thumbnail firmly across the paper. Thermal paper leaves a dark mark where you scratched it; bond paper stays unchanged.

Conclusion: Match the Paper to the Job

For most small hospitality businesses, the answer is straightforward: thermal for customer-facing receipts and terminals, bond for any ticket that must survive heat, light, or long-term storage. Buy the paper your printer was built for, and jams and faded printouts stop being a daily headache.

Your next step: confirm each printer's spec, stock the matching rolls, and keep a spare case on the shelf so you never swap in the wrong paper mid-shift.
